RUBBER TRADE
BIG JUMP IN AMERICAN IMPORT VALUES.
QUANTITY LESS:

The United States Chamber of Commerce announces that in the course of an analysis of the United States world trade the imports of crude rubber during the first half year increased by 117 per cent. in value, but the quantity showed only eight per cent, increase.
The average price per lb. in 1925 was $34½ cents compared with 69½ cents from January to June, 1926, when the value of the total imports was $322,000,000; —Reuter's "American Service.

STALIN.
$ _{1} $ NEW RULIER OF RUSSIA.
IS POLITICAL BOSS OF OLD TYPE.

London, September. 13.—Behind the kaleidoscope of Soviet politics, which recently has sent some well-known figures tumbling, stands a new power in the person of Stalin, the name he took which means the "Man of Steel." He is the Russian counterpart of an American political boss, the head of the machine, the power behind the principal actors of the Soviet drama to-day according to reports reaching England!

He sent Trotsky into exile and called him back again. He directed Djerjinsky, the head of the ferocious Cheka, the secret police, who recently died under mysterious circumstances. He sent Zinoviev down from power and was behind the dismissal of Kamenev from his place as chief of the Commissariat of Trade. His name is Josef Djugnashvili, but he calls himself Stalin.

He is a big man and dour. He is a blustering, rough and impetuous leader, who wins through discipline. Lenin was his first idol and still is his example. But Stalin is a practical man of politics, who does not let fine theories stand in his way. He recognises facts when he sees them, yielding here and pushing forward there according to the facts.

In his hands, Soviet Russia probably is on the edge of many changes, which will make it fit more smoothly into the society of other nations, for Stalin is neither a bigot nor a fanatic. He does not beat his head against stone walls.

He has made himself deliberately a man of greatest mystery. For years he boasted that he had never given out an interview for newspapermen, nor allowed any newspaper stories to be published about him if he could prevent them. He is the most difficult man in all Moscow to meet and now he is the most important. But Stalin is the despair of newspaper correspondents.

He has been a revolutionist since 1905 when he took active part in bloody fighting in the Caucasus, for which he was arrested by the Tzar's police and axiled to Siberia. But he came back with Lenin and worked for several years, quietly and smoothly, in the second rank of the leaders. He has only recently come forward to the front of the Soviet directors. His work until now has been almost unseen and wonderfully successful.

It was his task, when the Soviet Union was formed, to placate the so-called "outer nationalities," the states surrounding the fringes of central Russia which were declared free and independent by the Soviets but which had, above all else, to be kept within the Soviet circle. By adjolery, by adept leadership, by wise concessions and softness where softness was needed, he kept all the surrounding states except his native state of Georgia loyal to the Soviets. He used no force. The people chose to be loyal.

Then Stalin was promoted to become secretary of the Communist Party, which controls the Soviet Government, and there again his fine diplomacy, good judgment and political sense won for him a conspicuous success. He is gathering the fruits of it now, for his secretaryship gave him control of the Soviet political machine, the "steam roller" which he has now steered over the earlier leaders.
LIFEBOAT SIGHTED
NO SHIP REPORTS LOSS.
The Chinese Steamer “Haiyan,” from “Hoihow,” reports having sighted a white lifeboat in a position approximately 30 miles south of Gap Rock.

The "Haiyan" was not "bound for Hong Kong but being compelled to replace her funnel, lost during the height of the blow, and have other repairs effected she made the report on her arrival.
Up to the present no report of loss of a life boat has been made by any vessel caught in the typhoon and successful in reaching port.
IRISH COURTSHIP.
SYSTEM THAT CLOSELY RESEMBLES THE JAPANESE.

Courtship in Ireland is not the simple affair that it is in some countries. For Paddy, always a politician, has an eye to the main chance. And somewhere he has read that beauty is only skin deep. Rarely does he become engaged to a girl who has nothing but looks in her favour. In fact, his courtship is hedged round "by preliminaries that would cool many a girl's ardor.

Having noticed a girl whom he would like to marry; Pat does not proceed to make love to her. That would create a scandal. Instead; he usually seeks a go-between to plead his cause and to approach the father, whose consent is always necessary before a young man may even walk out with a young girl. This go-between or matchmaker often called the "mountainy-man," is found in every village and is almost invariably endowed with unlimited audacity and speech, as though he had kissed the Blarney Stone.

The matchmaker first insidiously creates an atmosphere. He talks with the girl, telling her what an "iligant feller" Pat is and what a nifty cottage he has on his two acres, "wid'a new thatch o nut, so it has." Also the cow, the pigs and the hens. Then he talks about it in the shop and in the saloon till at the countryside knows that Paddy wants to marry Bridget Malone. Then certain that Bridget's father has heard the rumour and has had time to think it over, the "mountainy-man" sallies forth with the swain to the father's house, a large bottle of best Irish, provided by the prospective bridegroom, in his pocket. He begins by reminding the father that it is high time his daughter got married and follows it up with the suggestion that if she doesn't hurry about it, he will surely have to keep her all her life.
“Sure Bridget will soon be on the shelf if you don't watch out,” he warns the father.

"And what way would she be lavin' this house, yet," retorts the father, "with her only a slip of a girl only just 20? It'll be a sorry day for me when she goes, for there's not the likes of her at making butter or cakes this side of County Tipperary."

Then, over many glasses of whisky and much good-humoured banter, the matchmaker cleverly ascertains how many cows and pigs the father is likely to give with his daughter when she does marry, and pointing to the young man who has remained silent throughout the conversation, he indicates what a fine son-in-law he would make and what a grand home his farm would make for the cows, the pigs and, incidentally, the girl. Finally, if both father and matchmaker are satisfied that they can strike a good bargain, they clinch the deal over another glass, and the father goes to the door, behind which the daughter has been listening all the time, and brings her in, protesting and giggling, to a seat near her sweet heart.

And so the two become engaged and after a short courtship are married, the wedding festivities providing a further occasion for bouts of merry-making, after which the bridegroom and his friends leave the bride in her father's House till the morrow, when with his best horse and cart he goes back to fetch her to her new home. At the same time his friends bring carts to take away the cows and pigs that form her dowry. An Irish country marriage is rarely improvident, and woe betide the father who fails to carry out any part of his verbal contract concerning the marriage settlement. An attorney in County Kildare not long go received a visit from an irate husband one week after his marriage. The latter wanted the father-in-law informed that the daughter would be sent back immediately if the promised cow was not delivered within three days. The animal was handed over.
POSTAL THEFTS.

YOUTH TEMPTED BY CINEMA
PICTURES.
MAGISTRATE'S LENIENCY

The case in which two clerks at the Post Office were charged with the theft of postal packets concluded before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy yesterday.
Mr. D. McCallum, who appeared for the Chinese defendant, said that in spite of a message sent to Macao the defendant had not returned, and he would therefore leave the matter in His Worship's hands. The ball of $100 was estreated.

On behalf of the Indian defendant, Mr. Leo D'Almada made a strong plea for leniency by pointing out that the defendant was young and was tempted to take the packets which contained pictures of cimena stars. Defendant, he said, had been dismissed from the service; had been disgraced, and it would be difficult for him to obtain employment in the future. In conclusion he asked His Worship not to send defendant to prison for what was after all "a youthful offence.

Addressing the defendant, His Worship said he had done a stupid thing, but he would be let off this time. He hoped it would not occur again. Defendant was bound over in a sum of $100 to come up for judgment when called upon.
SHANGHAI COUNCIL
Mr. S. M. Edwards, Municipal Secretary.
Shanghai, Oct. 1: Mr. S. M. Edwards, who has been acting secretary to the Shanghai Municipal Council since April 1 has been appointed secretary.—Reuter.

X-Ray Apparatus.
In reply to question by Dr. Koch as to whether the room in which X-Ray apparatus (for which there was a vote of $1,836.20) is kept was suitable for such apparatus, the Colonial Secretary said that he would make a note of the question and pass it on to the P.C.M.O.

No Harbour Pipes.
Arising out of a vote for $60,000 for laying pipes from Sheklaipai Reservoirice Reservoir to Kowloon Point, in connection with the Shing Mun Valley Scheme, Mr. Bernard asked if this included the cost of pipes to be laid across the harbour.
The Colonial Secretary replied that it did not. This part of the scheme was in abeyance.

Delicate Instruments.
Arising out of a vote for providing buildings for magnetic instruments at Au Tau, New Territories (amounting to $14,000). Mr. Bird asked if special preneurships had been taken in this building to protect the instruments from the difficulties of the climate.

The Hon. D. P. W. replied that the building, which was underground, had been specially constructed with the view to this and specially designed in accordance with the requirements of the Observatory authorities.
LEFT CHUNGKING
SEVENTY-SIX REFUGEES REACH HANKOW.
EXCITING TRIP DOWN RIVER

Hankow, Sept. 24—That matters are not all well up river was evidenced yesterday morning by the return to Hankow of a party of seventy-six residents of Chungking, who had been obliged to evacuate that city. This party consisted of Dr. and Mrs. Anderson and family, Mr. and Mrs. Irish and family, Mr. and Mrs. Bayne and family, Dr. Birke and family of the Canadian Mission. Mrs. Burcell and children, Mrs. Frier, and Miss Perkins of the same mission were also members of the party but remained in Ichang. Of the Chinn Inland Mission there were Dr. and Mrs. Parry, Mr. and Mrs. Batstone, Miss Shoering, Miss Cecil-Smlth, Mr. and Mrs. Burgess.

Mr. A. Davidson and Miss Hutchinson of the Friends Mission. Of the business people evacuated there were Mrs. Lewis and G. Lewis of the A.P.C., Mr. and Mrs. Pennyard of Mackenzie and Co., Mr. B. Hicks of Arnhold & Co., Ltd., Mrs. Donelly and three children, Mackenzie & Co., Mr. and Mrs. Wilson and child, A.P.C., Mr. and Mrs. S. B. Starling, of B. and S. remained in "Ichang" Mrs. Moying and Mrs. Hughes of Barry and Dodwell also remained in Ichang, Mrs. Jones of the Standard Oil Company also remaining in Ichang, Mrs. Bollard, of Brunner Mond and Co., to Hankow.

These people were warned on Friday night, the 17th inst., that they would be required to evacuate Chungking on the following day. It appears that a large demonstration was expected to take place that day in which it was feared that anti-British feeling might get beyond the control of the authorities and at a meeting it was decided to evacuate the place.

Previous to this, General Wang who was in command, had been able to give all assurance for the safety of foreign lives and property; but apparently there had arisen a difference of opinion between General Wang and two other Generals in the district, and the former had become a little uncertain of his powers.

The demonstration as planned, was to consist of the entire student body supported by the local militia from the surrounding districts; but in the event it is reported that the militia did not turn out in the numbers expected, and in consequence the demonstration did not reach the heights of violence expected.

During the absence of the British Consul, who was at Wanhaien, the United States Consul in the port arranged the evacuation, and is still holding bouts in case the Americans should eventually have to evacuate as well.

The evacuation was not quite the simple matter it would at first sight appear to be. Conditions down river were not definitely known, and in the first instance two steamers belonging to Jardine Matheson and Butterfield and Swire, respectively, with the refugees aboard, dropped down to the A.P.C. installation, some eight miles below Chungking.
The Journey Down.

The journey however was not continued on these boats as it was by "no" means certain that the Chinese, knowing that the "chung-king party, were on board, would not commence hostile demonstrations en route.

The following day, therefore, the steamers anchored at a point away from all villages on the banks, and were transferred to the Standard Oil tanker 'Mei Chuan,' and on this boat they proceeded on their journey.
At every point, en route, where there was a town or village or a
the party were on board, and this continued until after Wanhaien was passed.

Judging by reports the evacuation came none too soon; the population are definitely anti-foreign, and there is quite the possibility that the American citizens will also have to evacuate. Placards are reported as having been posted in the town stating that a certain Chinese society was prepared to pay the sum of one hundred dollars for every foreign head, and forty dollars for the head of every servant working for a British family.
Such a situation gives rise to a good deal of anxiety with regard to the safety of the large number of foreigners who reside in the interior of Szechuen. Reports have come to hand which indicate that the murderer of Mrs. Sibley was not the maniac that the authorities made him out to be but a member of the same society which is doing all the mischief at Chungking.
COSTS

AVOIDANCE OF REGULATIONS
When Sir Frederick Lewis, in the course of his annual address to the shareholders of Messrs. Furness, Withy, and Co., spoke of the saving in operating costs resulting from transferring a ship to a foreign flag, it is perhaps a pity that he did not go into greater detail. Presumably he was referring both to the saving in wages and the avoidance of many of the regulations that are imposed on British shipowners. The economy in wages would not necessarily infer a reduction of individual wages, as the law entails the upkeep of a larger crew in British ships than is required abroad. I believe that no country in the world, except our own Dominions and the United States, insists on the maintenance of as large a crew on board ship as is required under British law, and many shipowners hold very strongly that the law could be relaxed without any danger to life or limb and with pronounced benefit to our sea-carrying trade.
Apart from regulations as to crew, not even the United States has such an elaborate code of shipping laws as Great Britain. A number of our regulations have been strongly criticised—as, for example, our timber-carrying regulations, which have been condemned as being very much more costly than Continental regulations but not as effective in their purpose. Such a prominent shipowner as Lord Kylisant has argued that in the present emergency the Board of Trade would be well advised to review all our shipping regulations with a view to curtailing them temporarily until such time as the industry can afford to carry a heavier burden than is imposed on their foreign competitors. It seems clear that Sir Frederick Lewis's views cannot be very different from Lord Kylisant's.

The actual saving that Sir Frederick Lewis quoted in the particular case of a steamer that was recently transferred to a foreign flag amounted to $247 a month, or round about $3,000 a year. From these figures one gathers that the steamer is not a very large one, as the saving of foreign regulations

In comparison with British regulations is known to be substantial. He quoted a number of examples of speedy dispatch abroad. In the United States one vessel recently loaded 9,000 tons of cargo and 1,500 tons of bunkers within twenty-four hours. On the Continent a grain cargo of 7,100 tons was discharged in two days. These are two examples out of several showing performances that are rarely equalled at our own ports. Sir Frederick Lewis pointed out that ships are probably the highest valued instruments of commerce, and it would make an enormous difference if they were all handled in port with the speed and economy that is achieved abroad.

It is interesting to notice that efforts are now being made to bring down the cost of loading coal—that is to say, of loading coal when British coal is once again on the market. At the time of the Coal Commission shipowners, contended strongly that a big impediment in the coal export and bunker trade was the high cost and difficulty of loading coal. They particularly complained of the trimming charges, on which a reduction is at present being sought. After several meetings it is announced that the National Joint Trimming Committee has been unable to arrive at any agreement, on future wages, and that notice has been given of a reduction of the present tariff that is to be put into operation on Monday week.

It may be recalled, however, that in addition to the question of charges, shipowners found themselves in difficulty, according to the evidence given before the Coal Commission, with the refusal to coal trimmers to work a third shift. The absence of night work since the war was proved to lead to serious delays not only to coal ships, but also to general cargo vessels, resulting in a bill of expenditure that ought to be avoided. The difficulty arose out of a somewhat complex situation, and the Coal Commission suggested that a conference of all the parties concerned ought to be able to tackle the whole matter and find a convenient solution. So far it does not appear that any steps have been taken towards calling such a meeting.
All in all, it is only too clear that before the shipping industry is rehabilitated much work still remains to be done. Unfortunately, so many of the difficulties are contributed from outside the industry. They are not alone adding to operating costs, but many of them are responsible for diminishing our export cargoes, and thus making a double difficulty to always.
